itemdesc-wingfabric: Linen sealed with wax or resin until it is taut and windproof. Stretched over the wing spars of a flying machine.
itemdesc-wingspar: Planks glued end to end with resin into one long, light beam. The backbone of a wing.
itemdesc-wing: A full wing: spar, stick ribs lashed with twine, and doped fabric stretched over it all. A biplane needs two.
itemdesc-cylinder-*: A finned cylinder hammered from two ingots. The ribs shed heat so the engine does not seize. An engine needs two.
itemdesc-crankshaft-*: A shaft forged from two ingots with a pair of throws bent opposite ways. It turns the pistons' push into the spin of a propeller.
itemdesc-engine: Two cylinders bolted over a crankshaft in a riveted iron crankcase, packed with rendered fat so it does not grind itself apart. The heart of a flying machine.
itemdesc-propeller: Four planks laminated with a jug of hot pitch glue and carved into two twisted blades. It bites the air the way an oar bites water.
itemdesc-chaindrive: Two gears salvaged from the ruins and a length of iron chain, greased so it runs smooth. Carries the engine's turn back to the propeller.
itemdesc-wheel: Planks pegged into a solid disc around an iron axle rod, greased so it turns freely. A flying machine rolls on two of them until it is fast enough to fly.
itemdesc-trestles: Sawhorses and a coil of rope to fence off the yard. Set them down on flat, open ground to start building a flying machine there. The yard is 9 by 9 blocks and needs 5 blocks of open air above it.
itemdesc-copperwire: A copper ingot sawn into thin strands and wound into a coil. Carries current from a battery to the lamps on an instrument panel.
itemdesc-battery: A sealed jug of water and crushed sulfur with a lead plate and a copper rod standing in it. It gives off a steady trickle of current, enough to light the warning lamps of a flying machine.
itemdesc-dashboard: A plank board set with five gauges behind window glass (speed, compass, altitude, fuel and climb) and a pair of warning lamps. Fitted into a flying machine together with a battery to light the lamps.
site-notclear: Needs {1} blocks of open air above the whole building site
fuel-insert: Put in a container of Aqua Vitae
fuel-wrong: Too weak to burn. The engine runs on Aqua Vitae
fuel-busy: Someone else is filling the tank
nodismount-air: Too high to jump out. Land first
disassemble-occupied: Everyone must get out of the flying machine first
disassemble-cargo: The cargo shelf must be empty
disassemble-notlanded: The flying machine must stand still on the ground
handbook-flyingmachine-text:
The Flying Machine
Wood, linen and a hammered-iron engine. It flies, mostly.

A biplane for crossing great distances. Its parts are made at the workbench and the anvil, then put together one by one on a building site out in the open. It runs on Aqua Vitae and needs a long, clear stretch of ground to take off.

The parts
• Two biplane wings, each made from a wing spar, sticks, twine and doped wing fabric.
• An engine: two engine cylinders and a crankshaft, smithed from iron or better, bolted into an iron crankcase.
• A propeller, a chain drive and two landing wheels.
• An instrument panel (window glass, nails and strips, a plank and copper wire sawn from a copper ingot) and a lead-acid battery (a jug with 2 litres of water, crushed sulfur, a copper rod and a lead plate).

The building site
Craft flying machine trestles and rightmouse the ground with them. The site needs a flat, solid area of 9 by 9 blocks with 5 blocks of open air above it, and it faces the way you are looking. With block interaction help turned on (blockinteractionhelp), looking at the site shows what the next step needs. Keep those items in your hotbar and rightmouse the site. The steps, in order:
1. Frame: 8 support beams and 16 planks. The wood of the beams becomes the wood of the machine.
2. Landing gear: 2 landing wheels, 2 support beams and 2 iron nails and strips.
3. Lower wing.
4. Upper wing, with 8 sticks and 4 rope for the struts and bracing.
5. Engine.
6. Chain drive and propeller.
7. Tail: 8 planks, 2 doped wing fabric and 2 rope.
8. Instrument panel and battery.
9. Seats: 2 chairs.
Then rightmouse once more to roll it out. Trestles with nothing built on them yet can be picked up again with sneak + rightmouse and an empty hand.

Fuel
The tank holds 10 litres of Aqua Vitae. Weaker drink will not burn. rightmouse the engine with a bucket, jug or bottle of it to open the fuel tank and pour it in. At full throttle the engine burns about a litre a minute. When the tank runs dry the engine dies, and the machine glides.

Flying
rightmouse the front seat to take the controls. The rear seat carries a passenger.
• walkforward / walkbackward: throttle up and down. The throttle stays where you leave it. The engine needs a couple of seconds of cranking before it catches.
• jump / sprint: nose up and down. The nose also stays where you leave it.
• walkleft / walkright: bank and turn in the air, steer the tail wheel on the ground.
• sneak: get out. Only works on the ground, on water or a few blocks above them, so a slip of the finger cannot throw you out mid-flight.
Open the throttle fully and roll straight ahead. It takes about 30 blocks of flat ground before the wings can carry the machine; lift the nose gently once it is fast enough. Climbing costs speed and diving gains it. Too slow, and the wings stop carrying: the STALL lamp blinks and the nose drops on its own. Lower the nose to win back speed.

Landing
Throttle back, keep the nose a little down and let the machine sink onto its wheels. On the ground, hold walkbackward with the throttle closed to brake.

Instruments
Speed, altitude, fuel and a compass. The variometer shows how fast you climb or sink, in blocks per second: needle up for climbing, down for sinking, level at 0. It lags a moment behind, like the real thing. The battery powers the two warning lamps. The FUEL lamp lights when the tank runs low and blinks when it is empty.

Cargo
A chest, basket or crate fits on the shelf behind the pilot: hold it and sprint + rightmouse the shelf.

Taking it apart
Hold sneak + rightmouse on the machine with an iron, meteoric iron or steel wrench for five seconds. Everyone must be out, the cargo shelf empty and the machine standing still on the ground. You get back every part and material it was built from, trestles included, but the fuel in the tank is lost. Carry the parts to flat ground anywhere and build it again. A half-built site can be torn down the same way. Only the builder (whoever set out the trestles) can take a machine or site apart, along with server admins and anyone with build rights on land claimed where it stands. Anyone may fly it.
